    Layer-1 regime/state and halving features — implemented. Strategies that gate on market regime (regime-switch, mean-reversion gated on a ranging regime, volatility-regime rules) or on the halving cycle depend on two indicators: MARKET_STATE (regime as continuous + discrete + categorical + persistence columns) and HALVING. Both now exist across common / core / data-processing, with the MEGA generator wired (the full_single_tf_v2 / full_multi_tf_v2 groups use them in place of the market_regime signals). Their column set and build are in 20260622_REGIME_MARKET_STATE_AND_HALVING_PLAN.md. Expressing this class of strategies now only needs the rule layer to consume these columns.

    4. Backtest and Live Execution Model

    The backtest trades a single instrument: the experiment's base_symbol. Extra symbols are consumed only as context features; no positions are opened on them. Contextual multi-symbol (use ETH/BNB features to decide a BTC trade) is supported; portfolio multi-symbol is not. Execution realism is present: maker/taker commission split, slippage with variability, minimum-notional rejection, full investor metrics including benchmark and risk-constrained alpha.

    Live trading reuses the same bot decision code: runtime_loop calls the same generate_entry_signals / generate_exit_orders as the backtest, and the same apply_trailing_stops. LIVE_SIM fills orders through a simulated adapter; LIVE_REAL routes to a provider adapter whose submit_order is not yet implemented (providers return rejected), with no slippage, no partial close, and no persisted pending queue (Section 8.2).

    5. Bot Decision Flow

    The current bot has two decision paths:

    • generate_exit_orders: position-scoped management. It checks each open position and may emit a CLOSE order. The current fixed priority is stop loss / trailing stop → take profit → signal flip → uncertainty (side confidence below exit_threshold). Risk force-flat is applied in the engine loop after strategy exits, and optional end-of-window liquidation runs after the loop.
    • generate_entry_signals: portfolio-scoped entry proposal. It turns the model signal plus strength/quality into candidate entries gated by entry_threshold, min_quality_threshold, same_direction_cooldown_ticks, and require_higher_confidence. The risk manager then approves or rejects those proposals and calculates size.

    This split stays valid. The action engine does not delete the current bot. It adds an optional, declarative source of action candidates beside the current fixed logic:

    • With action_rules.enabled=false, the current bot behavior is unchanged.
    • With action_rules.enabled=true, the bot also evaluates configured predicates and maps matches to typed action candidates (CLOSE, REDUCE, ADD, REVERSE, ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT, and so on). Market-view entries stay Layer-1 model rules (they produce the cached signal); book-aware entries — that depend on the current positions / exposure / capital, which the model cannot see — are Layer-2 bot actions.

    When enabled, rule actions do not bypass the hard safety logic. The deterministic precedence per position is STOP_LOSS / TRAILING_STOP → TAKE_PROFIT → RULE_EXIT (rule-driven close) → SIGNAL_FLIP → LOW_CONFIDENCE, one exit per position per tick; risk-increasing rule actions (ADD and the open leg of REVERSE) still pass through the risk manager. Rules therefore intervene by inserting their candidates into this fixed order — never by overriding stops or risk approval.

    The three-class model signal still has no CLOSE: NONE means "do not open", it does not close a position. "Enter on A, exit on B" cannot be expressed as A -> LONG, B -> NONE; the exit must map to a bot action.

    6. Remaining Limitations

    The trailing stop, previously inert, now applies and persists per tick in both backtest (engine_loop.py, apply_trailing_stops) and live (runtime_loop), with a TRAILING_STOP exit code. Remaining limitations that this plan addresses:

    6.1 DSL / model limits

    • No function calls (abs, min, max); no rolling statistics inside an expression.
    • No position awareness inside a rule (entry price, bars-since-entry, unrealized PnL are available to the bot but not exposed to rule expressions).
    • No explicit CLOSE action; only NONE/LONG/SHORT.
    • strength/quality are constant for a whole rule set, limiting confidence-based sizing and pyramiding.
    • Rules use priority (first match wins), not voting.
    • The numbers inside rule strings are plain literals, not Optuna-optimized; parameter search is grids only.

    6.2 Flaws in the shipped rule configuration

    The previously-shipped configuration stacked classic rules in priority order. Two design problems make its negative results uninformative about rule viability: shadowing (with first-match-wins, the EMA fast-vs-slow pair captures almost every row, so MACD/ADX/Stochastic rules never fire) and state, not event (ema_9{-1} > ema_21{-1} detects a persistent state, not a crossover; a crossover needs two timesteps). These produce persistent directional signals, not discrete entry events.

    7. Target Architecture — Two Layers

    A professional trader answers two distinct questions every tick. The engine mirrors that with two layers, each isolated, with one clear responsibility and a well-defined interface.

    7.1 Layer 1 — Market view (the model) — unchanged

    Layer 1 answers "what does the market look like now?" and produces the signal LONG/SHORT/NONE plus strength/quality, from market features only. It is not position-aware. It is the model — rule_based (view by rules) or a trainable (view by network). Its output is cached in the prediction parquet and flows into the thesis pipeline and ensembles. This layer is not changed by this work; the training contract is untouched.

    7.2 Layer 2 — Action engine (the bot) — universal, position-aware

    Layer 2 answers "given that view and my current book, what do I do?" and produces actions. It is position-aware (open positions, unrealized PnL, bars-since-entry, free slots, exposure) and runs in the bot at runtime. It is a universal bot feature: it consumes the Layer-1 signal of any model — rule_based, mlp, tcn, vit — because the bot is shared by all models and does not depend on which model produced the signal. No model is modified to gain it.

    Today Layer 2 is a set of fixed gates plus fixed exit priority (Section 5). The target is an optional Bot Action Engine over the shared DSL. It evaluates predicates and emits typed action candidates with explicit scope and payload. The existing bot remains the default behavior when no action rules are enabled.

    Canonical runtime flow:

    1. The loop receives the feature row / candle, the current positions, and the latest portfolio state.
    2. The model produces the Layer-1 market view (LONG / SHORT / NONE, probabilities, strength, quality).
    3. The bot builds a rule context from market features, prediction values, market data, and position state.
    4. The bot evaluates optional action rules and fixed built-in logic, producing action candidates.
    5. The bot applies deterministic priority and conflict handling.
    6. The risk manager approves and sizes risk-increasing actions: the model-signal entry (as today) plus the Layer-2 risk-increasing actions (ADD and the open leg of REVERSE).
    7. The backtest or live runner executes the resulting orders.

    7.3 The shared rule DSL — rainbow.common.rules

    The expression evaluator currently lives inside rule_based.py (model-trainer). It is extracted into a new shared subpackage modules/common/src/rainbow/common/rules/ so both layers reuse one predicate engine without violating dependency direction (bot-logic must not import model-trainer).

    common.rules is a predicate engine, not a signal engine and not an action engine. It owns feature-token resolution, safe AST compilation, DSL validation, placeholder binding, and boolean evaluation of an expression against a supplied context. Feature-token resolution includes the standard alias matching used by all rule consumers: a rule can write a short stable alias such as rsi_14, and the resolver maps it to the one concrete feature name in the supplied context (for example rule_raw_BTC_5m_rsi_14) when the match is unambiguous. It returns whether an expression holds (a scalar boolean or a batch boolean mask). It does not know what a match means.

    Layer-specific payloads live with the layer that owns them:

    • Layer 1 keeps {expression, signal} rules. common.rules evaluates expression; model-trainer applies priority/default handling and maps the matched signal (LONG / SHORT / NONE) into logits.
    • Layer 2 keeps {expression, action, ...} rules. common.rules evaluates expression; bot-logic applies priority/conflict handling and maps the matched action payload into orders or management decisions.

    This keeps rule semantics shared without turning the shared DSL into a strategy, signal, or execution module.

    A compiled expression runs against a supplied variable context — either a batch context of market features (Layer 1, the model) or a single-tick scalar context of market features plus position variables (Layer 2, the bot). Both layers import the compiler, resolver, and placeholder binding from common.rules; the scalar evaluator is also shared from common.rules (bot-logic uses it for Layer 2), while the batch evaluator is the torch backend owned by model-trainer (Layer 1). One compiler and one resolver, in the foundation layer, shared.

    common.rules stays torch-free: it owns feature-token resolution, AST compilation, DSL validation, placeholder binding, and the scalar evaluator. Layer 1's batch backend — which executes a compiled expression over a torch.Tensor feature block and returns a boolean mask per predicate — lives in model-trainer (the layer that already owns torch), built on the shared CompiledExpression produced by common.rules. The rule intelligence (parse / compile / validate / bind) is shared in the foundation layer; the tensor execution backend sits with the code that owns the tensor. The model layer still owns signal payloads, first-match / default handling, and logits.

    The DSL is expressive — operators live in the DSL, heavy transforms live in features. The split rule: cheap, ad-hoc, short-window logic is a DSL operator; heavy, reused, or long-history logic is a precomputed feature that a rule just references.

    • DSL operators: single offsets feature{-1}; range selectors feature{-20:-2} and disjoint lists feature{-60:-50,-20:-1}; window aggregates over a range (highest, lowest, avg, sum, min, max, std, count, any, all); scalar functions (abs, min, max); event/series helpers (bars_since, cross_up, cross_down, change, pct_change, consecutive_true, slope, percentile); plus arithmetic, comparisons, and booleans.
    • Feature/signal layer (already rich — data-processing/signals/ provides crossover, z-score, threshold, and an expression-based condition signal): heavy or reused transforms — long-window z-scores, correlations, spreads, volatility-normalized series, regime labels, complex reused boolean conditions. A rule references these as ordinary features; it does not recompute them.

    This operator set is a superset of the current rule_based grammar (which rejects function calls and has no ranges), so the rule_based migration (Phase 1, run after the live ensemble) gains ranges and functions rather than staying at parity. Conditions such as NR7 or inside-bar then need no new feature — they fall out of the DSL (true_range{-1} == lowest(true_range{-7:-1}), high{-1} < high{-2} and low{-1} > low{-2}).

    7.4 Action set and payloads (Layer 2)

    Action rules are not "entry rules" or "exit rules" as separate systems. They are predicates plus bot-owned action payloads. The predicate answers "does this condition hold?"; the payload answers "what action should the bot candidate represent?"

    Actions have explicit scope:

    • Position-scoped actions are evaluated once per open position. target: current_position means the candidate applies to the position currently being evaluated.
    • Portfolio-scoped actions are evaluated once per tick / side. They do not target an existing position.
    • Risk-increasing actions must pass through the risk manager before they become orders.

    Initial action catalog:

    • CLOSE: position-scoped; requires target: current_position; closes the current position; no risk approval.
    • REDUCE: position-scoped; requires target plus reduce_size (a DSL formula in instrument units, e.g. position_size * 0.5 to close half); pure reduction needs no risk approval.
    • REVERSE: position-scoped; requires target and an optional sizing policy; the side to open is derived as the opposite of the position's side; the close leg needs no risk approval, the open leg does.
    • ADD: position- or side-scoped pyramiding; requires target / side and size_policy; risk-approved. Adding to an open position is position-aware, so it is a bot action.
    • ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT: book-aware entry — open a new position from a rule that depends on the current positions / exposure / capital (which the model cannot see). Risk-approved (sized + limit-checked), but skips the model-signal filters (confidence / quality / cooldown) because the rule already decided the direction. Distinct from a Layer-1 market-view entry (which the model produces).
    • MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP: position-scoped protective-level updates. The new level (new_stop / new_take_profit) is required — a literal price or a DSL expression (position_entry_price, market_current_price - market_atr * 2). There is no config for a moved level (stop_loss_config / take_profit_config set the level only at entry), so the rule must supply it. Uses the parameter value model (§7.7).
    • ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL: position-scoped trailing-stop reconfiguration. The trail_distance / trail_activation are optional values (a literal or a DSL expression); when omitted they fall back to the existing trailing_stop_config, and when present give volatility-adaptive trailing (e.g. market_atr * 2).
    • FLAT_AT_TIME: portfolio-scoped force-flat at a session boundary.
    • HOLD: portfolio- or position-scoped no-op.

    Selection, count, and shared context vocabulary (multi-position capability). Three capabilities let the action set work over a multi-position book:

    • Per-position selector. The position-scoped acting actions (CLOSE, REDUCE, ADD) carry an optional selector — rank_by (an expression), order (asc / desc), and limit (an integer N). The bot collects the open positions whose predicate holds, ranks them by rank_by, and acts on the top N (order: asc ranks worst-first, desc best-first). With no selector the action applies to every matching position (the default, and the only prior behavior). This expresses "reduce only the worst loser", "close the two weakest", or "add to the single best winner"; selection lives in the action layer, not in a cross-position DSL operator. HOLD is a suppressor and takes no selector.
    • Multi-open count. ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT carry an optional count (an integer): one rule opens that many positions in a tick (a ladder / scale-in / basket), each still sized and limit-checked by the risk manager. Several ENTER rules also stack — every matching entry rule proposes, in list order.
    • Shared context vocabulary. The book vocabulary (book_open_positions_count, book_long_positions_count, book_short_positions_count, book_open_notional) is available in every rule context — position, portfolio, and entry — so a position-scoped rule can also gate on the global book state, and an entry rule likewise. Market, prediction, and time vocabularies are available everywhere too; position variables exist only where a current position is in scope.

    Conflict resolution is by list order. Among the money-moving candidates on one position (CLOSE / REDUCE / REVERSE / model SIGNAL_FLIP / model LOW_CONFIDENCE), at most one wins, and the first matching rule in list order is chosen; hard safety (stop / trailing / take-profit / force-flat) always outranks them, and one protective modification may ride alongside (it moves no money). ENTER rules stack through the risk manager in list order until capital / slots run out. List order is the priority knob (an optional explicit priority number remains a later addition).

    Two kinds of entry, split by what they depend on. A market-view entry ("enter long when RSI < 30") depends only on the market, so it is a Layer-1 model rule ({expression, signal} in rule_based): it produces the LONG / SHORT signal with the model's strength / quality / confidence, is cached in the prediction parquet, feeds the thesis and ensemble pipeline, and flows through the model's entry gates. A book-aware entry ("enter long only if I am flat", "enter only if my exposure < X") depends on the current positions / exposure / capital — which the model cannot see — so it is a Layer-2 bot action (ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT). The model is never position-aware; everything that depends on the book lives in Layer 2. A book-aware entry skips the model-signal filters (the rule already decided the direction) but still passes the risk manager for sizing and limits — see the action-vs-filters rule in the Phase-4 design.

    Example shape:

    action_rules:
  enabled: true
  rules:
    - expression: "position_unrealized_pnl_pct{-1} < -0.02"
      action: "CLOSE"
      target: "current_position"
      desc: "Close current position after rule-defined loss"

    - expression: "position_unrealized_pnl_pct{-1} > 0.04"
      action: "REDUCE"
      target: "current_position"
      reduce_size: "position_size * 0.5"

    - expression: "position_side_long{-1} == 1 and position_unrealized_pnl_pct{-1} > 0.03"
      action: "ADD"
      side: "LONG"
      size_policy: "risk_manager"

    - expression: "position_side_long{-1} == 1 and trend_bearish{-1} == 1"
      action: "REVERSE"
      target: "current_position"
      size_policy: "risk_manager"

    The first implementation slice supports only the smallest useful payload: a position-scoped CLOSE action against the current position. That proves the rule-driven, position-aware management path while leaving the full action payload model for the next slices.

    Layer-2 actions complement the Layer-1 market view: Layer 1 says what the market looks like; Layer 2 decides what to do with the book. The model can still provide the default entry candidate source, and action rules can optionally add or override action candidates when enabled.

    A regime-switch strategy is expressible natively — conditions over the regime feature with and/or (e.g. regime_trend_trending{-1}==1 and cross_up(...) for the trend sub-policy, regime_range... for the mean-reversion one), no new engine capability; rule grouping would be optional sugar only. Note the order-layer cost (Section 8.1): CLOSE reuses the existing generic close path, but ADD, REDUCE, REVERSE, MOVE_STOP, and MODIFY_TP require new order actions and are scheduled in Phase 4.

    7.5 Parametric rules + Optuna over strategy parameters

    A rule predicate may carry tunable placeholders, e.g. rsi_14{-1} < ${rsi_buy}. A strategy declares a search space over its placeholders reusing the existing Optuna param kinds (Float/Int/Ranges/Categorical/log). Each trial binds the placeholders, builds the concrete predicates plus their layer payloads, runs the backtest, and is scored by alpha_rc/net.

    There are two optimizers, one per layer, because the layers live in different places and have different cost profiles. The native Optuna inside model-trainer today samples only the model and its training (learning rate, batch size, weight decay, loss, architecture, feature selection); it does not touch the bot, and for the non-trainable rule_based it optimizes nothing (the rule thresholds are fixed literals, so it runs a single deterministic trial). The bot-config optimizer (scripts/thesis/script_2_thesis/bot_config_optimizer) is a separate script that varies the bot_config over cached predictions. Strategy optimization maps onto these two homes:

    Layer What is optimized Optimizer Cost Status today
    Layer 1 (view / signal) entry-predicate thresholds and payload choices that change the signal extension of the native model-trainer Optuna — make it sample the rule placeholders for rule_based and regenerate the signal per trial (no training) regenerates the signal each trial; no training core support built — native rule_based hyperparameter resolution samples/binds rule params; signal-regeneration harness remains
    Layer 2 (actions / bot) action-predicate params + stops/TP/sizing (do not change the signal) the bot-config optimizer (script) over cached predictions re-backtest only, fast core support built — action-rule params/config cloning are available; optimizer script/harness wiring remains

    So optimizing the market view is an extension of the native model Optuna (it belongs to the signal flow); optimizing execution and management is the existing separate optimizer. Each layer keeps its natural home and reuses the shared param kinds and suggest_* machinery; neither is forced into the other.

    Overfitting control is mandatory and identical to a grid: tune in-fold, validate out-of-fold / on a held-out window, before any parameter set is believed. (The first profitable Jun-19 result is in-sample and unproven until validated out-of-fold.)

    7.6 A strategy as one object

    A strategy is defined in one place as {entry_rules (Layer 1), action_rules (Layer 2), param_space}. entry_rules are {expression, signal} payload wrappers around shared predicates; action_rules are {expression, action, ...} payload wrappers around shared predicates. At experiment generation they are deployed to their technical homes: entry rules to the model hyperparameters, action rules to bot_config. The single definition gives coherence; the split homes respect the cacheable-signal vs runtime-position-aware nature of each layer.

    This single-strategy object is an authoring / deployment construct, not part of the core engine. The type already exists — RuleStrategyConfig in modules/common/src/rainbow/common/types/configs/experiments/rule_strategy_config.py, exported from rainbow.common.types.configs — and validates the strategy-level parameter space and placeholder coverage (at least one entry or action rule; identifier-valid placeholder names; every placeholder backed by a parameter in param_space or action_rules.parameters) without owning model signals or bot actions. Do not delete or recreate it. It is Phase-3 scope: the core engine (Phase 1–2: the shared DSL, rule_based, and the optional action engine in backtest / LIVE_SIM) does not depend on it, and nothing consumes it yet. Phase 3 only needs to wire it — the generation step that splits one strategy into model hyperparameters (Layer 1) and bot_config action rules (Layer 2), plus the optimizer that searches its param_space.

    7.7 Action-parameter value model (the definitive, uniform form)

    Every value an action rule carries — a protective level, a trailing distance, a size, a count — uses one uniform value mechanism with a per-parameter typed domain, so the author has a single mental model and nothing is ambiguous. Configs are never modified by this work; they are only read as a default, and only where the engine already has a config for that exact value.

    The value source — three forms, one field per parameter:

    • A literal number — a fixed value in the parameter's own unit (a price, a trailing distance, a count). Not used for a size (see below).
    • A DSL expression (a string in the same field) — a formula evaluated each tick in the rule context. It is self-documenting about its base, because it names what it operates on: position_size * 0.5 is half the position, equity * 0.1 / market_current_price is 10% of equity in units, position_entry_price is the entry price, market_current_price - market_atr * 2 is two ATR below price. It composes and nests like any rule expression (abs(highest(high{-20:-1}) - close{-1})).
    • Omitted — falls back to the engine's existing config for that value, but only where such a config exists; where it does not, the parameter is required (see the table). The config is read, never modified.

    There is no _pct field and no generic ambiguous "size": a size is named in instrument units and is always a formula, so its base is explicit (position_size * 0.5, equity * 0.1 / market_current_price). The "fraction of what" question is answered by the formula itself, never by a bare number.

    Config fallback exists only where the engine computes that value today. stop_loss_config / take_profit_config set the stop / TP at entry — there is no config for moving a level, so MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP are required. There is no config for how much to reduce, so REDUCE is required. The sizing config (risk-per-trade / kelly / pyramid) computes an entry / add size, so ENTER / ADD fall back to it; and trailing_stop_config exists, so ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL fall back to it.

    Parameter Action(s) Meaning Unit / domain Forms allowed Omitted →
    new_stop MOVE_STOP new stop-loss level price > 0 number | formula required
    new_take_profit MODIFY_TP new take-profit level price > 0 number | formula required
    trail_distance ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL trailing distance > 0, in the trailing type's unit number | formula trailing_stop_config
    trail_activation ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL activation threshold > 0, in the trailing type's unit number | formula trailing_stop_config
    reduce_size REDUCE amount of the position to close instrument units, 0 < x <= position size formula only required
    add_size ADD amount to add instrument units > 0 formula only sizing config
    enter_size ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT per-position size instrument units > 0 formula only risk-manager / sizing config
    count ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT number of positions to open int >= 1 number | formula required

    Typed-domain validation, two stages. A literal is validated at config load; a DSL result is validated at runtime against the domain (finite, in range, integral where required). A non-finite or out-of-domain result rejects and audits the action — it never applies a bad value. An unset parameter with a config fallback takes the config value, which is in-domain by construction.

    Risk-increasing actions still pass the risk manager. For ENTER / ADD the size is the requested size; the risk manager always validates admissibility (max positions, exposure, affordability) and may cap or reject it. The rule decides direction and requested size; risk decides what is actually allowed.

    Implementation. One shared value type — float | str | None (literal number / DSL expression / config default) — plus a per-parameter validator and a single resolver: if set, use the literal or evaluate the expression; else read the config where one exists, or reject as required -> validate the domain -> typed value. The per-parameter validator enforces the table (a size rejects a bare number; a required parameter rejects an omitted value). The protective slice lands new_stop / new_take_profit / trail_distance / trail_activation and reduce_size; add_size / enter_size reuse the same resolver when their sizing default is connected.

    8. Impact Analysis

    8.1 Backtest decision and close paths

    Per tick, process_tick (engine_loop.py) runs: execute pending orders → resolve prediction → apply_trailing_stops → position-scoped exits / management → risk force-flat → portfolio-scoped entries → risk approval → queue orders; end-of-run liquidation runs after the loop. Today apply_trailing_stops is a standalone step that mutates and persists the stop directly, separate from the exit decision. Phase 4 folds it into the arbiter's protective channel — it emits a PositionModification candidate instead — so every protective change (automatic trailing and rule-driven MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP / trailing config) resolves through one arbiter, logs to one trade_modifications audit, and passes one live-real provider gate.

    Existing exit codes (common/types/trade_meta.py): STOP_LOSS, TAKE_PROFIT, TRAILING_STOP, SIGNAL_FLIP, LOW_CONFIDENCE, MANUAL. The action engine first plugs into the existing position-scoped close path because CLOSE already has complete execution support: build_close_order composes the typed order, and orders.py processes any CLOSE generically (slippage, PnL, persistence). The first action-rule close reason uses the RULE_EXIT exit code.

    General actions need more infrastructure:

    • CLOSE needs no new orders.py action.
    • REDUCE can be implemented either as a partial close order or as a dedicated order action, depending on the final execution contract.
    • ADD and book-aware ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT become risk-approved OPEN orders (the rule decides the direction; the risk manager sizes and limit-checks); model-signal entries already use the existing OPEN path.
    • REVERSE is a compound candidate: close leg first, risk-approved open leg second.
    • MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP need order/update paths for protective-level changes.

    Those broader order contracts are scheduled after the initial close slice.

    Execution per mode. In backtest and LIVE_SIM every action above executes through the same order paths — CLOSE today (generic close: slippage, PnL, persistence), and REDUCE / ADD / REVERSE / MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP once Phase 4 adds their order actions — so both modes stay the bar and must be perfect (costs, slippage, partial fills, sizing, metrics). In LIVE_REAL the same candidates are produced and routed to the provider adapter, but they are not executed: submit_order is not implemented (Section 8.2). Wiring stops at that boundary on purpose.

    8.2 Live (sim + real)

    Live reuses the same generate_exit_orders / generate_entry_signals, so the action engine is inherited by both live modes once the bot decision code carries it. LIVE_SIM is in scope and must be perfect: it fills via the simulated adapter (queued with latency, seeded slippage), so the action engine runs there at the same realism bar as the backtest. LIVE_REAL is out of scope to complete now — there is no exchange API / execution contract yet: submit_order is not implemented (providers return rejected), no slippage is applied, partial close is rejected, and the pending queue is not persisted across restart. The decision path is wired up to the provider-adapter boundary and left there; these gaps are recorded, not closed. This is deliberate, not a blocker: strategies are validated on folds in backtest / LIVE_SIM first, and LIVE_REAL execution, reconciliation, and the provider contracts are a separate, later prerequisite for going live (see "Scope and priorities").

    8.3 Model→bot contract and feature passing

    Layer 1's contract ({logits, strength, quality} and derived prob_*/combined_confidence) is unchanged — no close_signal is added to the model, so the prediction parquet, ensemble merge, and frontend types are untouched. Layer 2 needs the raw features of the tick and the position variables. The bot receives a typed feature context from the engine loop (backtest) and runtime loop (live); both already hold the feature row. Position-scoped candidates derive variables such as bars_since_entry, unrealized_pnl_pct, and entry_price from the current open position. Portfolio-scoped candidates derive variables such as free slots, current exposure, and side counts from the current book. Book-aware ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT variables that depend on capital (exposure, available equity, notional headroom) require the engine loop and the runtime loop to pass the live equity / portfolio state into the entry rule context — an explicit wiring step, not only the feature row already delivered for exits.

    8.4 Resume / pause state

    CLOSE/exit rules are stateless and need no new persisted state. Stateful actions (e.g. a per-position pyramid counter, or a "scaled out once" flag) must be persisted in the runtime state (resume_state.py backtest, runtime_state_json live) to survive pause/resume; the design keeps Layer-2 rule state explicit and serialized when an action requires it.

    8.5 Files touched vs not touched

    Touched Why
    common/rules/ (new subpackage) shared, torch-free predicate DSL: feature resolution, AST compiler, validator, placeholder binding, scalar evaluator
    common/types/trade_meta.py add RULE_EXIT exit code
    bot config models + config/experiments/bot.yaml optional Layer-2 action-rules config (nullable, like other optional bot sub-configs); absent → current fixed-gate behavior
    bot-logic/helpers/ + bot_logic.py evaluate and arbitrate action rules (compile once, reuse per tick)
    model-trainer/models/rule_based.py (+ batch backend) import the compiler / scalar evaluator from common.rules; host the torch batch evaluator over the shared compiled expression (no signal-behavior change)
    backtesting-engine/.../engine_loop.py, live-trading-runner/.../runtime_loop.py pass the feature context to the bot
    Optuna: bot_config_optimizer/config_space.py (Layer-2) + model-trainer Optuna (Layer-1) strategy-param search space
    tests across every touched module per-method, positive/edge/negative
    Not touched Why
    Layer-1 model contract, prediction parquet, ensemble merge, frontend TS no close_signal on the model
    orders.py, sim_execution.py, real_execution.py — for CLOSE CLOSE processed generically; ADD/REDUCE/MODIFY add new order actions in Phase 4
    the thesis pipeline / training Layer 1 unchanged

    9. Code Quality Contract

    Every change in this line meets the project standard; messy-but-working is not acceptable.

    • Typed objects, not dicts. Predicates, layer rule payloads, contexts, and results are Pydantic models / frozen dataclasses passed whole; flatten to columns only at the persistence boundary. Variable names follow the type (action_rule, not rule).
    • Placement by responsibility. Shared DSL in rainbow.common.rules (foundation layer); action helpers with the other bot-logic helpers; the exit code with the other exit codes; config sub-models with the other bot config. Dependency direction respected: bot-logic imports common, never model_trainer.
    • Reuse, do not duplicate. Reuse build_close_order/build_exit_meta_from_bot/build_exit_reason, the CLOSE path in orders.py, the Optuna suggest_value/suggest_override, the existing config-loading and param kinds. Extract the predicate DSL once and share it; never copy the expression evaluator into model-trainer or bot-logic.
    • No suppression, no legacy, no patches. Fix root causes; no type: ignore/noqa/pylint: disable; no _old/compatibility shims; remove what a change replaces.
    • Docs and comments as code. Full docstrings (params, returns, examples); comments explain the non-obvious why. No meta-language (no narrating changes, no before/after, no plan/phase references in code, docstrings, or commit messages).
    • Quality gates per file (src and tests): ruff check, mypy --strict, pyright clean, pylint ≥ 9.5, markdownlint for docs. Mirrored by the per-module linting-gate test.

    10. Test Plan

    Every new method has tests; every change is covered. Each unit is tested for positive, edge, and negative cases, following the existing per-module test layout and the linting-gate test that runs the quality gates over src and tests.

    • DSL (common.rules): parse/compile valid predicate expressions (positive); chained comparisons, negative timesteps, placeholder binding (edge); rejected AST nodes, unknown/ambiguous feature, out-of-range timestep, malformed placeholder (negative). Evaluate predicates against both a batch context and a single-tick position-aware context. Tests assert that common.rules returns booleans / boolean masks only; Layer-1 signals and Layer-2 actions are asserted in their owning modules.
    • Action engine (bot-logic): each action fires when its rule matches (positive); first-match/priority interaction with the fixed exits, exact-threshold boundaries, position-variable values at entry/edge (edge); no duplicate close of the same position, no entry while force-closing, action with no matching rule → HOLD (negative). Reuse of build_close_order verified (exit code RULE_EXIT, metadata correct).
    • Config: model loads from YAML with defaults; rejects out-of-range; absent block → fixed-gate default behavior unchanged.
    • Feature passing: the engine loop and runtime loop deliver the correct feature context to the bot; parity between backtest and live for the same inputs.
    • Optuna: search space samples valid configs; placeholder binding produces the intended rules; a Layer-2 trial reuses cached predictions while a Layer-1 trial regenerates the signal; objective reads the produced session metrics.
    • Resume: a stateful action's state round-trips through pause/resume unchanged.
    • Trailing-stop invariant: a regression test that locks the current trailing behavior (the stop moves and persists; TRAILING_STOP exit fires) so the rule-based work cannot silently regress it.
    • Datetime / timezone consistency (final audit): the whole system stores and computes in timezone-aware UTC, while the persistence layer (SQLite) returns naive datetimes on read. Every datetime that crosses the DB boundary or enters arithmetic is normalized through the shared ensure_utc / ensure_utc_optional helpers before any subtraction, comparison, or hour / minute / weekday extraction, so a naive (reloaded) value is never mixed with an aware (live) one. Covers position opened_at / closed_at in bot-action contexts (position_bars_since_entry, FLAT_AT_TIME session checks, the time scalars), order timestamps, and resume-state round-trips; each site has a test exercising the mixed naive-vs-aware case explicitly — the case that only crashes in live / resume and never in an all-in-memory test.

    11. Incremental Implementation Roadmap

    Build the abstraction once; deliver in slices so each slice is shippable and validated.

    1. Phase 1 — Shared DSL. Extract the predicate evaluator into rainbow.common.rules (feature resolver + AST compiler + context evaluator + placeholder binding). Migrate rule_based so model-trainer keeps {expression, signal} payload handling but imports predicate compilation/evaluation from common.rules. Tests + gates.
    2. Phase 2 — Bot Action Engine foundation and first close slice. Introduce optional action-rule config, feature-context passing, position-aware variables, and the first typed action candidate: position-scoped CLOSE against current_position. Existing hard exits keep first priority (STOP_LOSS / TRAILING_STOP, then TAKE_PROFIT); the first rule-driven close emits RULE_EXIT; model-derived SIGNAL_FLIP and LOW_CONFIDENCE remain after it. With action_rules.enabled=false, the current bot behavior is unchanged. Tests across backtest + live sim.
    3. Phase 3 — Optuna over strategy params. Parametric placeholders + search space; Layer-2 optimization over cached predictions (reuse bot-config optimizer); Layer-1 signal-regeneration loop; in-fold/out-of-fold validation harness.
    4. Phase 4 — General action candidates and order contracts (decided design). Extend the optional action engine with ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT (book-aware), ADD, REDUCE, REVERSE, MOVE_STOP, MODIFY_TP, ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL, FLAT_AT_TIME, HOLD — the maximum-flexibility design, with the core refactor accepted. Chosen after an adversarially-reviewed options study.
    5. Architecture: candidate + arbiter, two channels. Each tick the bot collects typed action candidates (from the fixed exits, risk force-flat, and the rule actions); a single arbiter resolves conflicts and emits the final actions, replacing today's "one exit per position, first-match-wins" control flow — the documented exit precedence and the no-rules early-return are preserved exactly. Two channels: fill orders (OPEN / CLOSE / REDUCE) that move money, and a separate typed PositionModification message for state-only protective changes (MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP / trailing) that by construction cannot touch PnL / equity / metrics. The arbiter allows several actions on one position in one tick (e.g. scale out and tighten the stop on the same bar).
    6. Arbiter decision logic (the heart). The arbiter turns the per-tick candidate pile into final actions by fixed priority layers — top wins, safety is absolute:
      1. Safety: stop-loss / trailing / risk force-flat (daily-loss, drawdown) → close the position and ignore every other candidate for it. Never overridden by anything discretionary.
      2. Take-profit: → close.
      3. One money-moving action per position: among CLOSE / REDUCE / REVERSE / model SIGNAL_FLIP / model LOW_CONFIDENCE, the highest-priority candidate wins — at most one (you cannot reduce and reverse the same position the same tick).
      4. One protective modification, alongside: if the position is not being fully closed, one MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP / trailing update rides along (it moves no money, so it cannot conflict with the layer-3 action).
      5. New entries (portfolio): model-signal entries plus rule ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT plus ADD plus the open leg of REVERSE all pass the risk manager (sizing + max-positions + exposure + affordability) in priority order, until capital / slots run out. Within any layer, ties break by rule priority (list order today; an optional explicit priority number is available). The whole resolution is deterministic.
    7. Action-vs-filters rule. A bot action is a decided action: it skips the model-signal filters (entry confidence / quality / cooldown — those judge the model's own signal), but it always passes the risk manager (it is your capital). Direction is decided by the rule; size and admissibility by risk. Only model-signal entries are gated by the model's confidence / quality.
    8. Execution contracts. REDUCE = split-on-reduce: close a child Trade row for the reduced size and shrink the surviving row in place — the only representation that keeps PnL / fees correct against the three row-counting metric layers; it must hold Σ entry_commission == original and Σ size == original, carry a distinct child exit code, and suppress the child's position-time-exposure interval. ADD = a risk-approved OPEN reusing the existing pyramid sizing (a new decayed row). REVERSE = ordered legs [CLOSE, OPEN] (the open leg fills next tick). Protective updates persist stop_loss / take_profit / trailing deltas through a service write.
    9. Mandatory safety / correctness. Protective updates are provider-gated in LIVE_REAL (routed through the provider request, which returns rejected; persisted only on accept); today's trailing-stop write is brought under the same gate (it is a pre-existing direct live-real write). REDUCE is implemented in all three execution paths (backtest, live-sim, and the live-real partial-close guard preserved). In-flight queued orders survive pause / resume (or the multi-leg actions are made resume-atomic) before REVERSE ships. MODIFY_TP / trailing updates get a persistence path covering take_profit and the trailing-delta columns. The ActionRuleConfig.action literal is widened in both its definition sites.
    10. Audit & DB consistency (extend the existing systems, do not reinvent). Every new action stays as auditable as today's exits, reusing the per-trade reason-JSON, the operational-gate counters, and the established nullable + backfill conventions.
      • Reason codes: ExitCode carries only codes that actually close a position — extend it with REVERSE_CLOSE (the full close leg); REDUCE already ships. Entry-side provenance is the action_origin marker on Trade (PYRAMID_ADD, REVERSE_OPEN), not an exit code. A protective modification is not an exit (it closes nothing), so its code (RULE_STOP_MOVE / RULE_MODIFY_TP / TRAIL_MOVE) lives in the trade_modifications audit record (below), never in ExitCode. Add matching buckets to the exit-reason distribution (ExitReasonStats / fetch_exit_reason_stats) for the new exit codes so they are counted distinctly, not lumped into other; the distribution recomputes from trades.exit_reason — no migration or backfill. The same fix must also break out the already-shipped non-stop/TP codes (FLAT_AT_TIME, RULE_EXIT, SIGNAL_FLIP, LOW_CONFIDENCE), which the current fetch_exit_reason_stats still lumps into other: the wiring covers every non-stop/TP code, not only the Phase-4-new ones.
      • Trade lineage + origin: add nullable parent_trade_id (self-FK), position_group_id, and an action_origin marker (ENTRY / PYRAMID_ADD / REDUCE_CHILD / REVERSE_CLOSE / REVERSE_OPEN) on Trade, plumbed through create_trade / open_position, so a split child, an add, and a reverse leg are traceable to their parent / group.
      • Protective-modification audit: a single child table trade_modifications records every protective level change uniformly — one row per change: trade_id (FK), origin (TRAILING / RULE), kind (STOP / TP / TRAIL), old_level, new_level, modified_at, and the modification code (RULE_STOP_MOVE / RULE_MODIFY_TP / TRAIL_MOVE). The current trailing-stop audit columns (initial_stop_loss, stop_was_trailed, *_activated_at / *_updated_at) plus the new initial_take_profit stay on Trade as the latest-state cache; the table is the full history a fixed column set cannot hold. The existing trailing moves log into this same table — one audit for trailing and rule moves, not two — which is also where today's direct trailing write is brought under the live-real provider gate. The survivor's original size on a REDUCE is the original_size lineage column (above). Audit-only: no money moves.
      • Operational counters: add the action counters (reduce_action_count, add_action_count, reverse_action_count, move_stop_action_count, modify_tp_action_count, trail_action_count, an arbiter-blocked count + a *_by_reason_json map) to OperationalGateMetrics and its runtime accumulator (with pause / resume serialization), pack them in build_investor_submodels, flatten them in both to_flat_session_columns, and record them in both loops — following the existing gate-counter pattern exactly. The _action_count suffix is deliberate: these count bot actions fired — rule decisions — during the session and persist as session-metric columns, distinct from the exit-reason distribution (ExitReasonStats, recomputed on demand from trades.exit_reason.code), whose own reduce_count counts closed trade rows that exited as a REDUCE slice. trail_action_count counts the rule decisions to configure trailing (ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL); the automatic trailing-stop slide is not an _action_count (it is mechanical and config-driven, not a rule decision) — it is audited in trade_modifications with origin = TRAILING and its exits are counted via the TRAILING_STOP code, so automatic versus rule-driven stays distinguishable without a per-slide session counter. The two answer different questions and only the action counters are persisted; the suffix keeps the flattened column unmistakable. Placement: the action counters live in the metrics JSON (canonical) and as flat backtest_sessions / live_sessions columns (the queryable session subset), but are not mirrored to Trial.stage3_* — a Trial.stage3_* column is justified only by a metric trials are ranked / filtered / selected by (Sharpe, Sortino, profit factor…), which an operational action count is not. The pre-existing stage3_risk_force_flat_count Trial mirror is dropped for the same reason (the autogenerate drops the column); the operational counters keep their backtest_sessions / live_sessions flat columns.
      • Migration + backfill: the schema change is made on the ORM models, and the Alembic revision is produced by alembic revision --autogenerate and reviewed before use (SQLite renders the column adds as batch operations under the hood), then applied with alembic upgrade — the revision is never hand-authored. It adds the new columns to trades, backtest_sessions, live_sessions (and optional Trial.stage3_* mirrors) as nullable=True with no server default; existing rows stay valid as NULL (the established convention — most gate counters are already NULL on historical rows). Counters reconstructable from trades.exit_reason.code get a backfill pass mirroring the existing risk_force_flat_count backfill; non-reconstructable ones (arbiter rejections) remain NULL by design. On historical sessions the action counters are effectively empty: these actions never ran before the action engine existed, so the backfill pass reconstructs nothing on old data (the honest historical value is NULL/0). The pass matters only for forward consistency and for any future re-run of an old config through the new engine. Add per-action structured success logs at the action boundary (today's per-trade logging is error-only).
    11. Resolved details. ADD-vs-max_concurrent_positions is a config flag (consume a slot or extend); REVERSE sizes the open leg off post-close equity; the REDUCE child carries zero entry-commission; an action-moved stop / TP is audited in trade_modifications with its own modification code (RULE_STOP_MOVE / RULE_MODIFY_TP) — it closes nothing, so it is never an exit code. The automatic trailing stop is folded into the same protective channel: apply_trailing_stops emits a PositionModification candidate instead of mutating and persisting the stop directly, so automatic and rule-driven stop changes share one arbiter, one trade_modifications audit, and one live-real gate. When both want to move the stop on the same tick the most-protective stop wins (nearest price, safety-first, whatever its origin); a rule MODIFY_TP always wins the take-profit (a deliberate decision with no safety ordering to defer to). The position-scoped acting actions (CLOSE / REDUCE / ADD) carry an optional selector (rank_by / order / limit) resolved by collecting matching positions, ranking, and acting on the top N; ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT carry an optional count for multi-open; and the book vocabulary is available in every rule context. Deferred until a strategy needs it: a full cross-source conflict model beyond one-fill-plus-one-protective per position per tick.
    12. Build order (each a complete vertical slice: config → candidate → order / modify contract → risk → audit (code / lineage / counter) → tests → gates → QA): foundation (candidate collection + the exit-channel arbiter + the lineage / origin columns and the reduce / add operational-counter columns, with one Alembic migration + backfill) → HOLD → FLAT_AT_TIME → ADD → REDUCE → protective (gated) — which builds the second PositionModification channel and the two-channel arbiter, folds the automatic trailing into that channel, and adds initial_take_profit, the trade_modifications audit table, and the move_stop / modify_tp / trail counters under a single Alembic migration at the end of the slice → REVERSE (after queue-resume) → datetime / timezone consistency audit (final). Each action wires in its own reason code, lineage / origin, and counter as it lands; the closing audit verifies every datetime crossing the DB boundary or entering arithmetic is normalized through ensure_utc / ensure_utc_optional before any subtraction, comparison, or hour / minute / weekday extraction, so a naive (reloaded) value never mixes with an aware (live) one.
    13. Phase 5 — Feature layer + catalog. Expose far more of the existing feature/signal system to rule experiments (today rule_raw exposes 14 raw indicators at a single timeframe — §3.1) across timeframes, periods, context symbols, and raw OHLCV. The classic indicator catalog is complete (34 indicators, §3.2): Williams %R, CCI, MFI, PPO, TRIX, Aroon and Parabolic SAR were already built, and Keltner, SuperTrend, Ichimoku, Choppiness plus the swing/structure features (fractals, pivots) were added on the existing mold (IndicatorType + typed config + composed warm-up + process_ / validate_ + dispatch + tests), each computed with polars and each lookahead-free. The MARKET_STATE and HALVING indicators this wave depended on are already built (across common / core / data-processing, with the MEGA generator wired): MARKET_STATE consumes pre-computed indicator columns and emits its full regime column set (continuous components, discrete one-hot state flags, a categorical state code, and persistence / transition columns); classify_regime_codes is the one shared regime classifier, and the offline regime scripts under scripts/analysis/regime/ import it instead of keeping their own copy (a single source of truth). Both are used at whatever timeframe the experiment config sets, exactly like any other indicator — existing multi-timeframe handling makes a higher-timeframe feature usable at the base timeframe, so there is no new alignment work. Column set and build are specified in 20260622_REGIME_MARKET_STATE_AND_HALVING_PLAN.md. The remaining Phase-5 work is therefore the rule_raw expansion — adding include_<name> entries and their feature blocks so the rest of the catalog is callable raw from rules (generator config, not engine work) — not new indicators. Then a Phase-0 control battery and the vetted battalion on folds → chronological holdout → multi-year (the multi-year step needs the data refresh + de-hardcoded folds noted in the master roadmap).

    12. Decisions and Open Questions

    Decisions taken:

    • All Layer-2 actions live in the bot, not in the model; the Layer-1 training contract is not touched.
    • Bot action rules are optional. With action_rules.enabled=false, the existing bot flow remains the default behavior.
    • Layer-2 action rules are predicates plus bot-owned payloads. common.rules evaluates the predicate; bot-logic owns action scope, target, payload validation, priority, and order mapping.
    • Position-scoped actions (CLOSE, REDUCE, the close leg of REVERSE) are evaluated per open position and target the current position unless a later payload model specifies otherwise.
    • Portfolio-scoped actions (ENTER_LONG, ENTER_SHORT, FLAT_AT_TIME, HOLD) are evaluated once per tick.
    • Entry is split by what it depends on: a market-view entry is a Layer-1 model rule ({expression, signal} in rule_based, cached); a book-aware entry (depends on current positions / exposure / capital, which the model cannot see) is a Layer-2 bot action (ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT). The model is never position-aware; everything that depends on the book is Layer 2.
    • A bot action is a decided action: it skips the model-signal filters (confidence / quality / cooldown) but always passes the risk manager. Direction is decided by the rule; size and admissibility by risk. Only model-signal entries are gated by the model's confidence / quality.
    • Risk-increasing actions (ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT, ADD, and the open leg of REVERSE), plus the model-signal entry, pass through the risk manager.
    • The arbiter resolves the per-tick candidates by fixed priority layers (safety → take-profit → one money-moving action per position → one protective modification alongside → risk-gated new entries), ties broken by rule priority. Deterministic; the documented exit precedence and the no-rules early-return are preserved.
    • Position-scoped acting actions (CLOSE, REDUCE, ADD) carry an optional selector (rank_by / order / limit): the bot collects the positions whose predicate holds, ranks them, and acts on the top N; with no selector it acts on every match (the default). This is how "reduce the worst loser" or "close the two weakest" is expressed — selection is in the action layer, not a cross-position DSL operator. HOLD is a suppressor and takes no selector.
    • ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT carry an optional count to open several positions from one rule in a tick; multiple entry rules also stack, each sized and limit-checked by the risk manager.
    • The book vocabulary is available in every rule context (position, portfolio, entry), alongside the market, prediction, and time vocabularies; position variables exist only where a current position is in scope.
    • Conflict resolution is by list order: among money-moving candidates on one position the first matching rule wins; ENTER rules stack in list order through the risk manager. List order is the priority knob.
    • The DSL is extracted to a new rainbow.common.rules subpackage and shared by both layers.
    • common.rules is a predicate engine only: it evaluates expressions to booleans / boolean masks and does not know Layer-1 signals or Layer-2 actions.
    • Layer 2 is a universal bot feature available to any model, not specific to rule_based.
    • Position-awareness is in scope from the start.
    • Optuna optimizes both layers; overfitting is controlled by in-fold tune / out-of-fold validation.
    • The DSL is expressive (range selectors + window aggregates + scalar and event functions); heavy or reused transforms stay in the feature/signal layer.
    • Phase 2 priority is deterministic: hard exits (STOP_LOSS / TRAILING_STOP) win first, then TAKE_PROFIT, then the first rule-driven position close (RULE_EXIT), then model-derived SIGNAL_FLIP, then LOW_CONFIDENCE.
    • Phase 2 exposes raw FAT-window market features plus synthetic scalar windows for current market, prediction, and position state. The first slice includes market_current_price, market_atr, prediction_confidence, prediction_strength, prediction_quality, prediction_combined_confidence, prediction_prob_long, prediction_prob_short, position_entry_price, position_size, position_unrealized_pnl, position_unrealized_pnl_pct, position_bars_since_entry, position_side_long, and position_side_short.
    • Track A (the classic indicator catalog) is complete: all 34 indicators exist on the shared mold — Williams %R, CCI, MFI, PPO, TRIX, Aroon and Parabolic SAR, plus the latest Keltner, SuperTrend, Ichimoku, Choppiness, fractals and pivots, all lookahead-free. The open item is exposing the rest to rule_raw.
    • Regime is exposed as the already-built MARKET_STATE indicator (companion HALVING): it consumes pre-computed indicator columns in data-processing and emits its full regime column set; classify_regime_codes is the one shared classifier and the offline regime scripts import it (single source of truth). It is used at a configurable timeframe like any indicator. Regime-switch is expressed with conditions over these features, not a grouping capability.
    • The torch batch evaluator and its dependency live in model-trainer; common.rules stays torch-free (resolver + compiler + validator + binding + scalar evaluator). Both layers share the compiler and resolver from the foundation layer.
    • The Layer-2 action-rules config is optional / nullable, like the other optional bot sub-configs — no Field defaults; an absent block means the current fixed-gate behavior. Model rule-parameter blocks are likewise optional and sourced from YAML.
    • The single-strategy object (RuleStrategyConfig) already exists (in rainbow.common.types.configs, file rule_strategy_config.py, exported) and is a Phase-3 deployment construct, not part of the Phase 1–2 core. Keep it — do not delete or recreate it; Phase 3 only wires it to its consumers (the experiment generator + the strategy-param optimizer).
    • The Phase-4 action engine is the maximum-flexibility design (decided after an adversarially-reviewed options study): a candidate + arbiter with two channels (fill orders plus a typed PositionModification for state-only protective updates), allowing several actions on one position per tick; the arbiter replaces the first-match exit chain while preserving the documented exit precedence and the no-rules early-return. REDUCE = split-on-reduce, ADD = pyramid OPEN, REVERSE = ordered legs; protective updates are provider-gated in LIVE_REAL (and today's trailing-stop write is brought under that gate). The core refactor is accepted. Full detail in the Roadmap Phase-4 entry.
    • The persisted operational action counters carry an _action_count suffix (reduce_action_count, add_action_count, reverse_action_count, move_stop_action_count, modify_tp_action_count, trail_action_count) to stay distinct from the exit-reason distribution (ExitReasonStats), whose reduce_count counts closed trade rows that exited as a REDUCE slice. The counters tally bot actions fired — rule decisions (including ADD / MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP / ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL, which leave no trade row or exit code at all) — and persist as session-metric columns. The automatic trailing slide is not a rule decision, so it carries no _action_count; it is audited in trade_modifications (origin = TRAILING) and counted at exit via TRAILING_STOP. The distribution is recomputed on demand from trades.exit_reason.code and is never persisted. They answer different questions and may diverge (e.g. a selector reducing several positions in one tick).
    • Metric storage has three tiers with a clear placement criterion. The metrics JSON (backtest_metrics / live_metrics) is canonical and holds every field. A flat session column (backtest_sessions / live_sessions) is added only for a metric that SQL filters / ranks / aggregates / displays at the session level (the queryable subset, kept consistent with the JSON). A Trial.stage3_* column is added only for a metric that trials are ranked / filtered / selected by (Sharpe, Sortino, profit factor, exposure) — performance metrics, not operational counts. Operational action counters therefore live in the JSON and the session flat columns but get no Trial.stage3_* mirror; the pre-existing stage3_risk_force_flat_count mirror is dropped to match the criterion.
    • The protective-modification audit is a single child table trade_modifications (one row per stop / TP / trailing change: origin, kind, old_level, new_level, modified_at, code), with the Trade columns (initial levels, trailing flags / timestamps, and the new initial_take_profit) kept as the latest-state cache. Trailing moves log to the same table — one audit for trailing and rule moves. A protective modification is not an exit: its code (RULE_STOP_MOVE / RULE_MODIFY_TP / TRAIL_MOVE) lives in that record, never in ExitCode (which carries only codes that close a position). The arbiter resolves it on a second PositionModification channel, distinct from the money-moving order channel, so a stop/TP move rides alongside the per-position money-moving action and by construction touches no PnL / equity / metric.
    • The automatic trailing stop is folded into this same protective channel: apply_trailing_stops emits a PositionModification candidate instead of mutating and persisting the stop directly, so automatic and rule-driven stop changes share one arbiter, one trade_modifications audit, and one live-real provider gate (today's direct trailing write moves under that gate). When both want to move the stop on one tick the most-protective stop wins (nearest price, safety-first, whatever its origin); a rule MODIFY_TP wins the take-profit (a deliberate decision with no safety ordering to defer to). The current trailing-invariant regression test guards the behavior across this refactor.
    • The protective-updates slice lands as code first — initial_take_profit, the trade_modifications table, and the move_stop_action_count / modify_tp_action_count / trail_action_count columns on both session tables — and is migrated by a single Alembic autogenerate at the end of the slice, never one migration per column. Historical rows stay NULL / 0 (these actions never ran before the engine existed), so no backfill is owed.
    • The existing fixed stop-loss / take-profit / trailing-stop mechanism (set from stop_loss_config / take_profit_config / trailing_stop_config) is preserved unchanged; the DSL protective actions are purely additive. The arbiter is the single merge point: the automatic trailing (the old mechanism, from config) and the rule-driven protective actions (the new DSL) both arrive as PositionModification candidates and are resolved together. With no protective rules configured the channel carries only the automatic-trailing candidate, so the result is identical to today's behavior (the trailing-invariant regression test locks it). The protective payloads follow the uniform action-parameter value model (§7.7): MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP carry new_stop / new_take_profit (a literal price or a DSL formula, required — there is no config for a moved level), and ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL carry trail_distance / trail_activation (a literal or DSL value that falls back to trailing_stop_config when omitted, since that config exists). The static config keeps working and the rule layer adds an optional dynamic (e.g. ATR-based) override.
    • Action-parameter values follow one uniform model, specified in full in §7.7: every value an action carries (level, distance, size, count) is a literal number, a DSL expression, or omitted — and an omitted value falls back to the engine's config only where one exists for that value (trailing, entry / add sizing); where it does not (a moved stop / TP, the reduce amount, the count) the parameter is required. A bare literal is allowed only where its unit is unambiguous on its own (a price, a trailing distance, a count); a size is in instrument units and is always a formula, whose base it states explicitly (position_size * 0.5, equity * 0.1 / market_current_price), so there is no "fraction of what" ambiguity and no _pct field. Each parameter declares a typed domain validated statically (a literal) and at runtime (a DSL result — finite and in domain, else the action is rejected and audited). Risk-increasing sizes (ENTER / ADD) still pass the risk manager: the rule's size is the requested size, risk decides what is allowed. The DSL composes and nests (abs(highest(high{-20:-1}) - close{-1})); rank_by is already a DSL expression and entry sizing is already config-formula-driven, so the model generalizes existing behavior.

    Open questions:

    • Whether Layer-1 and Layer-2 parameters are optimized jointly or in stages.
    • Per-symbol battalions vs contextual multi-symbol; lab folder name for the catalog.

    Pending follow-ups:

    • Script 2 generator / preflight is a boundary-validation follow-up, not Layer-1 core work. It may call common.rules to compile rule expressions against generated feature names, but it must not own DSL parsing, alias resolution, rule semantics, Layer-1 signals, or Layer-2 actions. Address it only when generator / preflight work is the active plan item.
    • Per-position market-state-at-open access (future, separate from the protective slice). A position cannot currently see the market features as they were when it opened: the entry meta stores the decision values (entry price, signal confidence / strength / quality, the ATR used, the levels) but no raw feature snapshot, and the DSL cannot reconstruct it — the feature{T} timestep is regex-parsed to a literal, so a dynamic index such as close{-position_bars_since_entry} is rejected. Two options if a strategy needs it: (a) persist a market / feature snapshot at position open and expose it as position-entry variables in the rule context; or (b) extend the DSL to allow a function / dynamic value as the timestep index, so an opened-bar offset can index back to the bar at entry. Decide and scope this on its own; it is not part of the protective-updates work.

    14. Parallel research: the strategy catalog

    Which strategies to implement is a separate research effort that defines the predicate/payload wrappers to express; it does not change the engine architecture above. A 50-strategy seed catalog exists (docs/_researchs/_RULE_BASED/), grouped by family and weighted by evidence: trend-following / breakout / time-series momentum are the strongest, trend-filtered pullback and intermarket confirmation next, and mean-reversion is useful but cost-fragile. Each strategy references one of eight reusable bot profiles (trend-rider, breakout, pullback, mean-reversion, intraday/VWAP, failure-reversal, spread/pairs, regime-switch hybrid) that template the management logic.

    Coverage with this plan (expressive DSL + the added indicators + the Layer-2 action engine): essentially the whole single-instrument catalog is expressible. NR7 and inside-bar need no new feature (they fall out of the DSL); the classic indicator catalog is complete (§3.2). The only strategy deferred by structure is two-leg pairs / spread execution — it needs synchronized long-short legs and shared-capital accounting (a portfolio-execution capability), not an indicator or a DSL feature. Regime-switch hybrids are expressible natively (conditions over a REGIME feature; no grouping needed), and session/VWAP strategies need session features plus FLAT_AT_TIME; both are achievable, not deferred by structure.

    Each strategy becomes one experiment, recorded in an experiment ledger with: strategy family, base-logic id, parameter variant, feature profile, symbol-context profile, execution profile, and source hypothesis. A strategy can use many predicates with different layer payloads (for example several entry predicates that map to LONG or SHORT, plus a default_signal, and separate bot predicates that map to action payloads). Robustness scoring (with deflated-Sharpe / PBO multiple-testing control) sees the whole tested family, not just the winners.
